code.source:
menu = {"starters": ["fish fry", "bhaji"], "mains": ["fish curry", "xacuti"]}
print(menu["mains"])
print(menu["mains"][1])
menu["desserts"] = ["bebinca"]
print(len(menu))

scenes.onScreen: The name menu tied to a dict whose values are lists
scenes.animation: Name tags pop in with their arrows to the objects (value and type shown, no addresses); when Python reads a name the arrow glows and the object lights up
scenes.narration: Here is the picture. One name, menu, tied to one dictionary. Each value in that dictionary is an arrow to a list object. And each list holds arrows to string objects. Nested data is just arrows that point at other objects. To read a deep value, you follow the arrows, one bracket at a time.

scenes.onScreen: students.py: each student is one record

scenes.narration: [HL 1] A list with two items, and each item is a dictionary. Each dictionary is one student record. [HL 2] Loop over the list. Each round, s is one dictionary. [HL 3] Pick its name and marks by key. Asha, eighty eight. Ravi, ninety two. [HL 4] Or reach in directly. Index one is the second student. Then the key name. Ravi.

code.source:
students = [{"name": "Asha", "marks": 88}, {"name": "Ravi", "marks": 92}]
for s in students:
    print(s["name"], s["marks"])
print(students[1]["name"])

shorts.title: Containers in containers
shorts.script: Containers can hold other containers. A dictionary value can be a list. A list item can be a dictionary. Think of a restaurant menu. The menu has sections, each section has dishes, and each dish has a price. Real data is almost always shaped like this. Learn to read it. Then web data, files, and records look familiar. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Data inside data.

shorts.title: Chain the brackets
shorts.hook: "To read a deep value, chain the brackets from the outside in."
shorts.script: To read a deep value, chain the brackets from the outside in. Menu, bracket mains, picks the list of main dishes. Add another bracket, and you pick one dish from that list. Each bracket takes one step deeper. If you get lost, print the pieces one at a time. Every step gives you something simpler to look at. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: One bracket, one step.

shorts.title: A list of records
shorts.hook: "A list of dictionaries is the most common shape for data."
shorts.script: A list of dictionaries is the most common shape for data. Each dictionary is one record, like one student, with a name and marks. Loop over the list, and in each round pick the fields by key. Add a new student by appending a new dictionary. It is a tiny database, and you already know how to read it. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Records in a list.

shorts.title: Nested key error
shorts.script: Here is the bug. You reach into a nested dictionary, but the first key is missing. Python says, key error, drinks, before it even looks at the index. Use get with a default, like an empty list, then check that it is not empty before you go deeper. Defensive reads save you from crashes on real data. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Guard each step.

shorts.title: Pun and challenge
shorts.hook: "Why did the data feel so deep?"
shorts.script: Why did the data feel so deep? It had layers upon layers. Your challenge. You have a dictionary called data. Inside it is a key asha. That key holds another dictionary with maths eighty and science ninety. Print Asha's science mark. Use two sets of brackets, outside in. You should see ninety. Share your answer in the comments below. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 36.
shorts.caption: Try nested data.
